scenes.tts: Why did Virginia's nesting eagle map change so dramatically? One survey map begins with only a few gold nest markers. A later, larger search is crowded with them. The searches were not identical, so the picture needs a careful explanation. The difference asks what changed.

Expand the outline inland and add markers while '2016: 1,070 pairs; larger search' appears. Keep a small 'schematic map' label.

scenes.tts: Start with the pressure on reproduction. D D T was a pesticide used to kill pests. It breaks down into D D E. That related chemical can make bird eggshells thin. Thin shells often broke while the parents sat on them. Other eggs failed to hatch. Fewer chicks joined the next generation.
scenes.caption: Start with the pressure on reproduction. DDT was a pesticide used to kill pests. It breaks down into DDE. That related chemical can make bird eggshells thin. Thin shells often broke while the parents sat on them. Other eggs failed to hatch. Fewer chicks joined the next generation.
scenes.visual: Carry the shoreline. Zoom to one gold nest. A red DDT block changes into a red DDE block, then approaches a large egg cross-section. The shell becomes visibly thinner and cracks. Label the pathway 'schematic'; show fewer gold chick icons.
scenes.narration: Start with the pressure on reproduction. DDT was a pesticide used to kill pests. It breaks down into DDE. That related chemical can make bird eggshells thin. Thin shells often broke while the parents sat on them. Other eggs failed to hatch. Fewer chicks joined the next generation.

scenes.tts: D D T was not the only problem. People destroyed nesting habitat, and some shot eagles illegally. The causes differed, but they pushed the same population downward. Fewer young survived, and fewer safe places remained for nesting pairs. Several pressures could act together.
scenes.caption: DDT was not the only problem. People destroyed nesting habitat, and some shot eagles illegally. The causes differed, but they pushed the same population downward. Fewer young survived, and fewer safe places remained for nesting pairs. Several pressures could act together.
scenes.visual: Zoom back to the carried shoreline. Red pressure arrows point from the DDE block to eggs and from shrinking green forest to gold nests. One nest dims without showing extinction. A downward gold population gauge moves slowly and remains labelled 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: DDT was not the only problem. People destroyed nesting habitat, and some shot eagles illegally. The causes differed, but they pushed the same population downward. Fewer young survived, and fewer safe places remained for nesting pairs. Several pressures could act together.

scenes.tts: Now remove the pesticide pressure and protect nesting forest. What should happen next? Will occupied nests jump immediately, or rise over many breeding seasons? Hold your answer while the shoreline stays in view. Picture the time needed.

scenes.visual: A teal barrier slides between the red pressures and the shoreline. Restore a wide green forest band. Center the question 'Jump now—or rise over time?' above the carried schematic shoreline; gold nests gently bob.
scenes.narration: Now remove the pesticide pressure and protect nesting forest. What should happen next? Will occupied nests jump immediately, or rise over many breeding seasons? Hold your answer while the shoreline stays in view. Picture the time needed.

scenes.visual: Keep the prediction question and carried shoreline. A small timeline cursor pulses without advancing; water shimmers and tree crowns sway.

scenes.tts: The count should not jump at once. The United States banned most uses of D D T. Laws protected eagles and their nests. People also protected nesting places. Together, those actions reduced known harms instead of creating adult eagles instantly. Protection changed the conditions for survival.

scenes.tts: Recovery still takes time. A pair may raise young, but young eagles need several years before breeding. Some eagles also die or meet new dangers. The pathway is possible, yet each loop from nest to new pair takes time. That delay shapes the curve.

scenes.visual: On the same shoreline, animate a gold adult pair beside a nest, then a chick, a flying young eagle, and a new pair. Move the timeline cursor through several unlabeled seasons during the loop. A few icons fade gently under 'death and new dangers'.

scenes.tts: Here is the rule. Remove the harm, protect what remains, and help ecosystems recover over time. In this case, pesticide pressure was reduced and nesting places had protection. The population could grow through many rounds of reproduction. Recovery depended on reproduction across many seasons.

scenes.tts: The survey counts rose over decades, with a small dip along the way. That pattern fits recovery, but it does not prove one action caused every added pair. Search coverage, weather, habitat, and several protections all matter when scientists interpret counts. A count is evidence, not a complete cause map.

scenes.tts: The eagle story shows a population responding after pressures eased. An entire habitat can face another barrier. Even when conditions improve, the organisms needed to restart it may be missing. That is where restoration enters the story. The next film follows it.
